questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, what is the key difference between exploratory and explanatory visualization?
options: Exploratory visualization is for the analyst's own discovery and does not need to be polished; explanatory visualization is for an audience, built around one chosen message, and polish matters
Exploratory visualization uses only numeric data; explanatory visualization uses only categorical data
Exploratory visualization is always done in Power BI; explanatory visualization is always done in Python
Exploratory visualization comes after you have decided your conclusion; explanatory visualization comes before you have looked at the data
Exploratory visualization requires interactive tools like Plotly; explanatory visualization requires static tools like matplotlib
There is no real difference; the terms describe the same activity at different stages of a project
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines exploratory visualization as many quick, rough charts made for yourself to find surprises and check assumptions, where polish doesn't matter, and explanatory visualization as a polished chart built around one chosen message for an audience.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D gets the sequence backwards — exploratory charts come first, while you're still forming conclusions, and explanatory charts come after, once you've picked the one message you want to communicate. Neither kind of visualization is tied to a specific tool, which is why this is the one wrong option that inverts Lesson 1's actual definition rather than just adding an unrelated constraint.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe published four small datasets, each with eleven (x, y) points and nearly identical means, variance, and correlation, that look completely different when plotted. This demonstration is known as Anscombe's ________.
questions.explain: Anscombe's quartet is the classic demonstration that identical summary statistics (same mean x, mean y, variance, and correlation) can hide wildly different relationships — a linear trend, a curve, an outlier-driven line, and a single point creating an entire correlation — which is exactly why Lesson 1 opens the course with 'always plot your data before you trust a summary of it.'

questions.prompt: A product manager wants to know whether weekly active users have been growing over the past 24 months. Per Lesson 2's question-to-chart framework, which chart should you use, and why?
options: A line chart, because the question is about a trend over time, and a line correctly implies that order and the values between points matter
A pie chart, because showing 24 months as slices of a whole makes the growth easy to see
A bar chart with no sorting, because categories should always default to bars
A scatter plot, because two numeric variables should always be plotted against each other
questions.explain: Lesson 2 classifies 'is X growing over time' as a trend question, and trend questions call for a line chart with time on the x-axis — a line implies order and continuity, which is exactly right for 24 consecutive months and exactly wrong for unrelated categories. A pie chart only works for a couple of slices showing parts of a whole, not a 24-point time series.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about color in charts, per Lesson 3.
options: A sequential palette (light-to-dark of one hue) is the right choice for a variable that runs from low to high, such as spend per customer
A diverging palette should be used for categories with no natural order, such as regions or product lines
A rainbow colormap is a safe choice for a sequential variable because its bright bands help readers see fine differences
Categorical palettes should generally be limited to about five or six distinct colors, grouping the rest into 'Other' or using small multiples instead
Because color is a visual cue, relying on red versus green alone is a safe way to show a diverging variable
questions.explain: Sequential palettes (light-to-dark of one hue) suit low-to-high values; diverging palettes are for values above and below a meaningful center, not categories with no order — that job belongs to a categorical palette. Rainbow colormaps create false boundaries, which is why the lesson recommends perceptually uniform maps like viridis instead. Categorical colors should stay around five or six so readers can still tell them apart. Relying on red versus green alone fails for the roughly one in twelve men with red-green color-vision deficiency, so it is never safe without a second cue.

questions.prompt: Match each question family from Lesson 2 to the chart type it calls for.
right: Scatter plot
Line chart
Bar chart (horizontal if labels are long)
Histogram or box plot
questions.explain: Lesson 2's framework: compare categories calls for a bar chart (horizontal when labels are long); a trend over time calls for a line chart, since a line implies order and continuity; the distribution of one numeric variable calls for a histogram or box plot; and the relationship between two numeric variables calls for a scatter plot.

plt.plot(months1, revenue1)
plt.title('Q1 revenue')
plt.plot(months2, revenue2)

questions.prompt: A developer wants two separate charts, one titled 'Q1 revenue' and one titled 'Q2 revenue', using matplotlib's pyplot style as shown. Why doesn't this code produce two separate titled charts the way the developer expects?
options: pyplot style tracks one 'current' figure and axes at a time, so without creating a new figure between the two plot calls, both lines land on the same axes and the second title call overwrites the first
plt.title() can only be called once per Python script, ever
plt.plot() automatically creates a new figure every time it is called, so this code actually does work as intended
Titles in matplotlib can only be set using ax.set_title(), never plt.title()
questions.explain: Lesson 5 explains that the pyplot style relies on matplotlib remembering which figure and axes are 'current' — calling plt.plot() twice without plt.figure() or plt.subplots() in between draws both lines onto the same axes, and the second plt.title() call simply replaces the first. This is exactly why the course uses the object-oriented style (fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.plot(...); ax.set_title(...)) for anything with more than one chart.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in matplotlib's model, a ________ is the whole canvas that can be saved to a file, while an Axes is one individual plot on it, owning its own x-axis, y-axis, and title.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 defines the Figure as the whole canvas (like a sheet of paper, savable as an image) and the Axes as one plot on that canvas — a figure can hold a single Axes or many, which is exactly what Lesson 9's subplot grids build on.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about seaborn, per Lesson 7.
options: seaborn draws onto matplotlib axes, so titles, labels, and fig.savefig() from earlier lessons still apply to seaborn charts
seaborn functions take a DataFrame with data= and then name columns for x, y, and hue, rather than requiring raw arrays
The hue argument splits a chart into separate, non-interactive static images, one per category
sns.heatmap() is typically used to visualize a correlation matrix, with a diverging colormap centered on zero for signed values
seaborn replaces matplotlib entirely, so importing matplotlib is unnecessary once seaborn is installed
questions.explain: seaborn draws on matplotlib axes (so matplotlib's figure/axes tools still apply), takes data= plus column names for x, y, and hue, and hue colors and legends groups within the same chart rather than splitting into separate images. heatmap() is exactly the right tool for a correlation matrix, especially with a diverging, zero-centered colormap. seaborn is built on top of matplotlib, not a replacement for it — Lesson 7 is explicit that 'seaborn does not replace matplotlib.'

questions.prompt: Match each seaborn function from Lesson 7 to what it is used for.
right: Shows the spread and potential outliers of a numeric variable across groups
Colors a grid of values, commonly used for a correlation matrix
Shows the distribution of one numeric variable, optionally split by a category with hue
Shows the relationship between two numeric variables, with points optionally colored by category
questions.explain: histplot shows a numeric variable's distribution, optionally split by hue; boxplot compares spread and flags potential outliers across groups; scatterplot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, often colored by category; and heatmap colors a grid of values, the standard way to visualize a correlation matrix.

questions.code:
fig = px.scatter(customers, x='orders', y='spend', color='segment')
fig.update_traces(marker={'size': 7, 'opacity': 0.8})
fig.update_layout(template='plotly_white', legend_title_text='Segment')
questions.prompt: What does update_traces change here, compared to update_layout?
options: update_traces changes the marks themselves (marker size and opacity here); update_layout changes the chart as a whole (template, legend title, axis titles, size)
update_traces and update_layout are interchangeable aliases for the same method
update_traces only works on bar charts, not scatter charts
update_layout changes the underlying data values plotted, while update_traces only changes colors
questions.explain: Lesson 8 draws exactly this distinction: update_traces styles the marks (here, marker size and opacity), while update_layout styles the chart as a whole — template, legend title, axis titles, margins, and so on. Neither call touches the underlying data.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a matplotlib GridSpec dashboard, per Lesson 9, in the order they actually happen in the code.
items: Create the figure with plt.figure(figsize=..., layout='constrained')
Call fig.add_gridspec(rows, cols) to define the grid
Call fig.add_subplot(gs[...]) for each panel, including one that spans multiple cells
Plot data onto each individual axes and give each panel a left-aligned title
Add an overall title with fig.suptitle(...) and save with fig.savefig(...)
questions.explain: Lesson 9's GridSpec pattern starts by creating the figure, defines the grid with add_gridspec, carves out each panel (including a wide one spanning gs[0, :]) with add_subplot, plots and titles each panel individually, and finishes with a figure-wide suptitle and savefig — exactly the order that produces a consistent, readable dashboard.

questions.prompt: Put these five stages of the EDA workflow, per Lesson 10, in their intended order.
items: Frame the question: what decision or model is this data meant to support
First look: check shape, types, missing values, and duplicates
One variable at a time: look at distributions, spread, and unusual values
Two or more variables: look at relationships, group differences, and correlations
Decide and record: what to clean, keep, investigate further, or now believe
questions.explain: Lesson 10 lays out a five-stage workflow — frame the question, take a first look, examine variables one at a time (univariate), then two or more together (bivariate/multivariate), and finally decide and record — while noting that it's a loop you circle back through, not a rigid one-pass checklist.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, what is the key practical difference between the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients?
options: Pearson measures linear association and is sensitive to extreme values; Spearman correlates the ranks of the values, so it captures any consistently rising or falling relationship and is more robust to outliers
Pearson can only be computed on categorical columns; Spearman can only be computed on numeric columns
Spearman measures linear association and is sensitive to extreme values; Pearson correlates ranks and is robust to outliers
Pearson and Spearman always produce identical values for any dataset without missing values
Spearman can only be used on exactly two columns at a time, while Pearson can summarize an entire table at once with .corr()
Pearson requires the data to be sorted first; Spearman does not
questions.explain: Lesson 14 demonstrates this directly: for orders versus total_spend, Pearson gave about 0.20 (dragged down by two extreme spend values) while Spearman, which correlates ranks instead of raw values, gave about 0.85 on the same data. The rule the lesson draws: whenever Pearson and Spearman disagree sharply, look for outliers or a curved relationship.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C is the same claim with the two coefficients swapped — it's Pearson that measures linear association and is outlier-sensitive, and Spearman that uses ranks and shrugs off extremes. Getting this backwards would lead you to trust the wrong number exactly when a dataset like the lesson's, with two huge spend values, needs the rank-based one instead.

questions.prompt: In the practice dataset, total_spend has a mean of 188.1 but a median of only 124.4, with a maximum of 9800.0. What does this gap between mean and median signal, per Lessons 10 and 11?
options: The distribution is right-skewed, likely pulled by one or more extreme high values, which is a signal to investigate further rather than trust the mean as 'typical'
The data must contain a calculation error, since mean and median are always required to be equal
It signals that the column is categorical rather than numeric
It means the standard deviation must be exactly zero
questions.explain: Lesson 10 flags 'mean well above the median plus a huge maximum' as a signal to investigate, and Lesson 11 confirms it: total_spend is dramatically right-skewed (skew of about 15.03), and the median — not the mean — is the better 'typical' value once a distribution is skewed this way.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about detecting outliers, per Lesson 15.
options: The IQR rule flags any value more than 1.5 times the interquartile range below Q1 or above Q3, the same rule a box plot uses to draw its whiskers
A z-score cutoff of 3 is always more sensitive than the IQR rule, for any dataset
z-scores can understate how many values are extreme when a few very large values have already inflated the mean and standard deviation
An outlier flag is itself a final verdict that the row should be deleted
Quantile-based rules like IQR tend to be more robust than z-scores for skewed data
questions.explain: The IQR rule mirrors a box plot's whiskers exactly. In the lesson's data, z-scores flagged only 2 rows versus the IQR rule's 19, because the two extreme values had already inflated the mean and standard deviation the z-score depends on — making z-scores the blunter, less sensitive tool here, not the more sensitive one. A flag is a question to investigate (using something like spend-per-order), never an automatic verdict to delete. IQR being quantile-based is exactly why it holds up better on skewed data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 14, whenever Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients disagree sharply for the same pair of columns, that is a warning sign to plot the pair and check for ________ or a curved (non-linear) relationship.
questions.explain: In the lesson, Pearson gave about 0.20 for orders versus total_spend while Spearman gave about 0.85 — a huge gap caused by two extreme spend values. The lesson's rule: a big Pearson/Spearman gap means look for outliers (or a curved relationship) before trusting either number.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Chapter 3 to what it actually means.
right: An outlier that also looks wrong or unusual for an identifiable reason, such as a data-entry error
A third variable that drives both things you are comparing, which can make an unrelated pair look associated
Clipping extreme values to a boundary, such as a chosen quantile, to limit their influence without deleting rows
Turning raw counts in a cross-tabulation into within-row rates, so groups of different sizes can be compared fairly
questions.explain: A confounder is a third variable driving both sides of a comparison (Lesson 13's warning before trusting a two-variable story). An anomaly is an outlier that also looks wrong for an identifiable reason, distinct from a merely large but plausible value (Lesson 15). Winsorizing clips extreme values to a boundary instead of deleting them (Lesson 15's options list). Normalizing a crosstab by 'index' turns counts into rates so differently sized groups can be compared (Lesson 12).

rates = customers.pivot_table(index='region', columns='channel', values='churned', aggfunc='mean')
# South/app cell = 0.35, the highest in the table

questions.prompt: The South/app cell in this churn-rate heatmap is the darkest at 0.35, but switching aggfunc to 'count' shows that cell represents only 20 customers. What should you conclude, per Lesson 13?
options: The 0.35 rate is a lead worth investigating further, not a finding to report yet — a rate built from only 20 customers can swing a lot from just a few individuals
The cell should be reported immediately as the strongest finding in the dataset, since it is the darkest color on the heatmap
The small sample size means the cell should be deleted from the table entirely
A heatmap cell's color only reflects count, never the aggregated value, so the darkness is unrelated to the 0.35 rate
questions.explain: Lesson 13 explicitly warns to check the cell sizes behind a colorful rate: a dark cell built from only 20 customers (here, South/app) 'is a lead, not a finding' because a rate from so few people can swing substantially from just a handful of individuals changing status.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about automated EDA tools like ydata-profiling and Sweetviz, per Lesson 16.
options: They can quickly surface housekeeping issues like missing value counts, duplicate rows, and strongly correlated columns
In the lesson's run, the alert list automatically named the two implausible 9,800 and 7,400 spend values as anomalies needing a closer look
sv.compare() can put two dataframes side by side, such as a train and test split, optionally highlighting how each variable relates to a target column
An automated profiling report is a finished analysis, ready to paste directly into a stakeholder-facing document
Automated tools can miss context-dependent problems, such as a value being implausible for a specific business, which still requires hands-on reasoning to catch
questions.explain: The lesson's own run of ydata-profiling caught the 20 missing ages, zero duplicates, and the orders/total_spend correlation automatically — but its alert list did not flag the two suspicious 9,800 and 7,400 spend values; catching those needed the spend-per-order reasoning from the outliers lesson, which needs business context the tool doesn't have. sv.compare() is specifically built for comparing two dataframes, such as train/test, against a target. The lesson is explicit that a report is 'a set of observations, not a story' and should never be pasted to stakeholders as the analysis.

questions.prompt: A data scientist needs a Power BI report that stays current with the source database every time it's opened, even though this makes the report noticeably slower and limits some Power Query transformations. Which Data Connectivity mode should they choose when connecting to SQL Server, per Lesson 17?
options: DirectQuery, because it leaves the data in the source and queries it at report time instead of taking a snapshot
Import, because it copies the data into the Power BI file for the fastest performance
Python script, because only Python connections can refresh automatically
Publish to web, because it is the only mode that queries a live database
questions.explain: Lesson 17 contrasts the two modes directly: Import copies data into the file (fast, full feature support, but a snapshot until refreshed), while DirectQuery leaves data in the source and queries it live at report time — staying current at the cost of speed and some Power Query restrictions, which is exactly the trade-off described here.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a Power BI Python visual, or inside a Power Query 'Run Python script' step, the current table is handed to your script as a pandas DataFrame named ________.
questions.explain: Lessons 17 and 18 both use this exact convention: the table already loaded into Power Query or into the visual arrives in your script as a DataFrame named dataset, and any DataFrames you create become the step's or visual's output.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about sharing a Power BI report, per Lesson 19.
options: Sharing a report also shares access to its underlying semantic model, not just what's visible on the report page
Hiding a column, visual, or page from a report is a valid substitute for row-level security
Publish to web makes a report public on the internet with no authentication required, including the underlying data
Republishing from Power BI Desktop replaces the semantic model in the service with the updated one from the file
Edits made to a report inside the Power BI service are automatically saved back into the original Desktop file
questions.explain: Lesson 19 is explicit that sharing exposes the semantic model, not just the visible page, and that hiding elements is not security — row-level security is the real tool for restricting what different viewers see. Publish to web is called out specifically as making a report public with no authentication. Republishing does replace the service's semantic model, but changes made in the service are never saved back to the original Desktop file.

questions.prompt: Match each Power BI sharing need from Lesson 19 to the approach it calls for.
left: Show one report to a few named people
Give a whole team a polished, read-only experience
Work on a report together with teammates, with different roles
Discuss findings where people already talk day to day
right: Publish an app from a workspace
A workspace with roles such as Admin, Member, Contributor, and Viewer
Teams integration
A direct link, using the Share button
questions.explain: A direct link via Share suits a few named people; publishing an app from a workspace gives a team a polished read-only view; a workspace with Admin/Member/Contributor/Viewer roles supports collaborative work on the report itself; and Teams integration puts findings where people already talk.

questions.code:
rates = [11.3, 14.9, 26.0, 44.7]  # churn % for 0, 1, 2, 3+ tickets
ratio = rates[3] / rates[0]
questions.prompt: Lesson 20's chart is titled '3+ tickets: ~4x the churn.' Where does the '4x' number actually come from?
options: It is the computed ratio of the churn rate for 3+ tickets (44.7%) to the churn rate for 0 tickets (11.3%) — about 4.0 — never an eyeballed estimate
It is an industry-standard benchmark unrelated to this specific dataset
It is the number of tickets being compared (0 versus roughly 4)
It is the difference between the two percentages (44.7 minus 11.3), rounded
questions.explain: Lesson 20 is explicit that you must compute the number you put in a title, never eyeball it: 44.7% divided by 11.3% is about 4.0, which is where '~4x' comes from. The lesson also warns to state group sizes alongside the ratio — 248 customers had zero tickets and 103 had three or more — so the claim can be judged, not just believed.

questions.prompt: Put these four parts of a presentation to a non-technical audience, per Lesson 22, in the order they should appear.
items: The answer: state the finding in one clear sentence up front
The evidence: one or two charts, each titled with a finding
The caveat: one honest slide on what the data does not prove
The ask: a specific, concrete recommendation or next step
questions.explain: Lesson 22's four-part flow puts the answer first so the audience isn't kept waiting through methodology, follows with evidence (charts titled as findings), adds one honest caveat about what the data can't prove, and ends with a specific ask — exactly the structure applied again in the capstone wrap-up.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 21, a written analysis should put the ________ first, with a summary that could stand alone even if a busy reader only reads two sentences, and only then give the evidence behind it.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 flips the order analysts usually work in: rather than load-clean-explore-model-conclude, a write-up should lead with the answer and recommendation, then supply the question, data, findings, caveats, and next steps for anyone who wants the detail.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about staying honest in a data story, per Lesson 20.
options: Showing that high-ticket customers churn more does not by itself show that tickets cause churn
Reporting a rate without its denominator (the group size behind it) hides how much data the finding actually rests on
If you examined ten different breakdowns and only report the one that looked dramatic, you should say so
Because the story is about one dataset, strong words like 'proves' are preferable to hedges like 'suggests'
A chart should never highlight one bar in a different color, since that counts as manipulating the reader
questions.explain: Lesson 20's honesty guardrails: association is not cause, rates need their denominators shown, and cherry-picked breakdowns need to be disclosed as such. The lesson recommends hedges like 'suggests' over strong claims like 'proves' for a single dataset — the opposite of the fourth option. And highlighting one bar with a strong accent color while greying out the rest is one of the lesson's own explicit techniques for a chart that carries a message, not manipulation.

questions.code:
ct = pd.crosstab(df.region, df.churned)
p = chi2_contingency(ct)[1]
# p = 0.037
questions.prompt: The capstone's chi-square test on region versus churn returned a p-value of 0.037, just under the usual 0.05 line. Given that four different variables were tested this way, how does the build lesson say you should treat this result?
options: As weak evidence worth watching, not yet convincing — when you scan several variables, a few will cross the significance line by chance, and in this case the dataset's own generating recipe confirms region played no real role
As the strongest finding in the whole analysis, since 0.037 is a smaller number than 0.05
As proof that region directly causes churn, since the test came back statistically significant
As evidence that the test itself was performed incorrectly, since a real effect must produce a p-value under 0.01
questions.explain: The build lesson treats the region finding as 'worth watching, not yet convincing': 0.037 barely clears 0.05, and after testing four variables some will cross that line by luck. Because the dataset was generated from a known recipe, the lesson can confirm directly that region plays no part in it — the East gap was a live demonstration of exactly this kind of chance result, which real data wouldn't let you peek behind.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the capstone's 800-customer dataset, the baseline churn rate established in the kickoff lesson — 157 of 800 customers — was approximately ________%.
questions.explain: 157 of 800 customers churned, which the kickoff lesson computes as about 19.6%, or roughly one customer in five — the baseline every later pattern (tickets, tenure, plan, region) gets compared against.

questions.prompt: Match each item the wrap-up lesson says to package for a portfolio to what it should contain.
right: Opens with the question, the answer, and one image, then links to further detail
Restarts and runs top to bottom, with dead ends removed and narrative in Markdown cells
Where the data came from, what each column means, and known issues — stated plainly if the data is generated
The random seed, library versions, and how to run the analysis
questions.explain: The wrap-up lesson's portfolio checklist: a README that leads with the question, answer, and one image; a cleaned notebook that runs top to bottom with the narrative in Markdown; a data note on source, meaning, and known issues; and reproducibility details — seed, versions, run instructions — so a stranger can trust and rerun the project in minutes.
